lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. One of the things I like about summer is I have the opportunity to do a little bit of extra reading. And I try not to read only new books. Sometimes I do like to read some that are a bit older. And so in that vein, I recently finished reading Robert N. Thompson's memoir, A House of Minorities, which was originally published in 1990. Now, at this point, you're probably wondering, who's Robert N. Thompson? The answer is that he was a former member of Parliament who served as leader of the Social Credit Party from 1961 to 1967. However, that probably still doesn't help most of you. You see, few people today remember the Social Credit Party. And yet Social Credit used to be a force to be reckoned with in Canadian politics. Social Credit began as a provincial party in Alberta during the Great Depression. Originally led by William Aberhart, a radio preacher who later became Premier, he was succeeded by Ernest Manning, the father of future Reform Party leader Preston Manning. People in other provinces soon took notice of this new party. and formed their own. In 1952, W.A.C. Bennett led his Social Credit Party to victory in British Columbia and served as Premier of that province for the next 20 years. While Social Credit never formed government in any other province, they did exceed in electing some provincial MLAs, including right here in Manitoba. Thompson came to prominence when he became leader of the federal Social Credit Party in 1961. and was elected to Parliament in 1962. This gave Thompson a front-row seat to one of the most notorious political rivalries of all time: Progressive Conservative leader John Diefenbaker versus Liberal leader Lester Pearson. In the 1962 election, Diefenbaker's massive electoral majority was reduced to a thin minority of only 116 out of 265 seats. Since Thompson's Social Credit Party had 30 seats, this effectively gave Social Credit the balance of power. Unfortunately, Diefenbaker had little interest in working with Thompson, even though they both shared similar small-c conservative values. According to Thompson, Diefenbaker blamed him for splitting the vote and costing him his majority. Diefenbaker's minority government didn't last long. On February 6th, 1963, Thompson voted with the rest of the opposition parties for a non-confidence motion and brought down the government. In the subsequent election, Pearson won a minority government with 128 seats, while Social Credit was reduced to 24 seats. However, Thompson faced strife within his own party. While Thompson had long abandoned the original Social Credit economic theory of the 1930s, his Quebec wing had different ideas. And since most Social Credit MPs came from Quebec, this put Thompson in an untenable position. In 1963, the party split, with most Quebec MPs forming the Réellement Décréditiste under the leadership of Réal Couette. Interestingly, Thompson's political career was not finished yet. He tried to merge his party with the Progressive Conservatives. And when this attempt failed, he crossed the floor and joined the Progressive Conservatives in 1967, which were then led by new leader Robert Stanfield. Thompson was re-elected in his Red Deer riding in 1968, where he served until his retirement in 1972. It is ironic that for 4 years Thompson served in the same caucus as his former rival, John Diefenbaker. It's too bad they didn't get along better. Since they had many things in common. One thing that stood out to me from Thompson's book is how much things have changed in politics since his time. As an obvious case in point, the Social Credit Party is no more. As another example, Thompson had described Saskatchewan as a stronghold for the NDP. Of course, that has since changed, since Saskatchewan hasn't elected a single federal NDP MP since since 2015 and hasn't had a provincial NDP government in 2007. Thompson died in 1997, and few people remember him today. That is unfortunate, since there is much we can learn from our former political leaders. Whether we like it or not, change is a constant in politics, whether we're at the federal level, the provincial level, or the municipal level like we are here today. It's a good thing for us all to remember. Thank you.

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Variance application file V-2024-07, Yes. The variance application is being applied for, for property with an address of 101-103 Winston Place. The owner of the property is [name withheld], with the applicant for the variance being G&E Homes. Purpose of the variance application is to allow an 18-foot, 2-inch rear yard setback, whereas the RMD residential medium density zone requires a minimum rear yard setback of 25 feet. To be able to construct a covered deck at the rear of the dwelling at 103 Winston Place. The existing— or the planned structure for the site is a duplex. With respect to the application, as I mentioned, it is a side-by-side duplex that is proposed for the subject property. A copy of the site plan is provided for council's information. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Hrehirchuk. Council has received the application and the agenda package showing the configuration and proposed location of the covered deck. Administration has provided several examples of past precedents where council has considered similar applications, with all of those precedents previously having been approved. of both the rear and side yards of the subject property. Recommendation from administration is for council to approve the application subject to any new evidence being presented.
